title: Hand-tap an M6 tool hole in a robot tool adapter plate: start it square, back it off every turn, back it out
instruction: Tap an M6 thread right through the hole ringed in blue on the robot's tool adapter plate, with the tap in the T-handle wrench. Start the tap square to the plate and keep it square, without pushing the wrench sideways. Break the chip as you go: after every turn in, turn the tap back at least a quarter turn. Stop when the red band on the tap reaches the plate, then turn the tap all the way back out and stand the wrench back in its stand.
context: Robot wrists end in a standard tool flange (ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 on Universal Robots' e-Series and Franka's FR3, "DIN ISO 9409-1-A50"). Tools often have another footprint, such as ISO 9409-1-63-4-M6, so builders make adapter plates from aluminium stock: the plate bolts to the flange through clearance holes, and the tool's screws go into M6 holes tapped by hand, the part in a vise and the tap in a tap wrench. NIMI's fitter course (Exercise 30): "The tap alignment should be corrected within the first few turns"; "Any extra pressure on one side will spoil the tap alignment and can also cause breakage of the tap"; "Turn backwards frequently, about quarter turn, to break the chip." The robot must start the tap within 2° of square, regrasp the wrench every half turn within its ±120° wrist without pushing the tap sideways, and reverse regularly. Not tested: drilling the hole or choosing the tap.
setup: Frame: Two YAM arms with parallel grippers; bases 61 cm apart at the table's near edge. Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. Nothing is random. Vise (fixed): A Wilton 11744 4 in low-profile drill-press vise, cast iron, 5.4 kg, bolted to the table with two M10 bolts through its base slots. Jaws 102 mm wide, along y, centred at y −14.85. Jaw tops 7.3 cm up, 38 mm jaw depth. Screw along x, handle away from the robot, fixed jaw toward the robot. The jaws' inner faces grip the plate at x 24.0 and 32.0. Base as drawn: x 19 to 45, y −22.35 to −7.35. Parallels: two hardened steel parallels, 150 x 32 x 3 mm, on edge on the vise bed along y, one against each jaw. Workpiece: a tool adapter plate for a robot wrist, made in-house. A 6061-T6 aluminium disc, 80 mm across and 6.0 mm thick, turned from round bar, deburred, about 85 g. Robot face (underneath), for an ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 flange: a centring spigot 31.5 mm (h7) across and 3 mm high; four 6.6 mm screw holes on a 50 mm circle at 45°, 135°, 225° and 315°, countersunk 90° to 12.4 mm on the tool face for M6 ISO 10642 screws; one 6 mm (H7) dowel-pin hole on that circle at 0°. Tool face (on top), for an ISO 9409-1-63-4-M6 tool: four holes on a 63 mm circle at 22.5°, 112.5°, 202.5° and 292.5°, each drilled 5.0 mm through, square to the face, and countersunk 90° to 7.0 mm. The hole to tap is ringed in blue paint marker (a 12 mm ring); the other three are left for later trials. It rests on the parallels, gripped across a diameter, tool face up and flush with the jaw tops (7.3 cm up), turned so that the marked hole lies on the line through its centre parallel to the jaws, on the −y side. Its centre is at (28, −14.85) and the marked hole at (28, −18). Below the hole the plate is clear down to the vise bed. Tap: An HSS M6 x 1.0 D3 straight-flute plug hand tap, bright, 4 flutes (Regal Cutting Tools 020169AS, about US$10). 63.5 mm long, 25.4 mm of thread, 6.48 mm shank, 4.85 mm square, plug chamfer of 3 to 5 threads (drawn: 4), 12 g. A red paint-marker band 2 mm wide round its thread, its lower edge 13.5 mm above the tip (it reaches the plate when the tap has advanced about 10.2 to 11.6 mm, depending on how deep the point first sits). Its chamfer is wetted with aluminium tapping fluid. Wrench: A Starrett 93B T-handle tap wrench (taps 4 to 6.4 mm, squares 4 to 6.4 mm), steel, holding the tap by its square. As drawn, to be matched to the bought wrench: knurled body 65 mm long and 20 mm across; sliding T-bar 6.4 mm across and 100 mm long, centred, its axis 7 mm below the body's top; 70 g. The tap stands 55.5 mm out of the body, so the T-bar's centre is 113.5 mm above the tap's tip. Stand: A grey PLA block 40 x 40 x 60 mm, centred at (18, −30), with a 12 mm hole through its centre, chamfered 45° to 24 mm at the top. It is fixed to the table with double-sided foam mounting tape under its base. The wrench stands in it: the body rests on the chamfer (lower end 5.8 cm up) and the tap hangs in the hole, tip 2.5 mm above the table. The T-bar lies along x. Start: Both grippers open at the ready pose.
scoring: Real-trial tools: overhead and wrist video; an M6 x 1.0 6H GO thread plug gauge; an M6 x 60 mm threaded rod (DIN 976); a 75 mm engineer's square; feeler gauges. Square: With the plate still in the vise, turn the rod into the hole by hand until 5 to 10 mm shows below the plate. While each gap is read, pull the rod's top end straight up, lightly (about 10 N), to seat its flanks; never push it sideways. The engineer's square stands on the plate's top face against the rod at four positions 90° apart. The largest gap 40 mm up must be 1.40 mm or less (the thread within 2.0° of square). Simulation: the thread's axis, which is the tap's mean axis over its first turn after it bites. Through: The GO gauge screws through the plate by hand. Simulation: the tap advanced 10.0 mm or more, which puts its band at the plate. Started: The GO gauge screws in at least 2 full turns. Simulation: 6.0 mm or more. Back-off: Turning the tap back by 90° or more. Chip run: new thread (deeper than before) cut since the last back-off. From the overhead video a judge allows 10° for reading the T-bar's angle: a back-off counts from 80°, and a chip run fails only beyond 370°. The simulation uses 90° and 360°. Latched 0 at any moment: The tap snaps: Video and inspection. Simulation: 1.5 N·m of bending at the plate's face (about 14 N sideways on the T-bar) or 5 N·m of twist while in the thread. A chip run of more than one full turn: Overhead video. Also 0: a crooked thread (not square), or a thread not started. Otherwise, at the end: 1.0: Through and square, tap out of the hole (its tip 2 mm or more above the plate, or 6 mm or more from the hole's axis), the wrench standing in its stand (tap tip in its hole, within 15° of vertical), both grippers 3 cm or more from it and the wrench still (under 1 cm/s), for 1 s. 0.75: Through and square, tap out, the wrench anywhere else. 0.5: Through and square, tap still in the hole. 0.25: Started and square, not through. 0: Anything else, or any latch.
reset_notes: Adapter plate: One fresh pre-drilled hole per trial, so one plate gives four trials. Plates are made in batches beforehand: turned from 80 mm 6061-T6 round bar (about US$5 of bar each), with the spigot, then every hole drilled, countersunk and deburred as drawn (about 20 minutes each). About US$1.25 of material per trial. Before each trial, ring the next untapped hole in blue paint marker and clamp the plate on the parallels, tool face up and flush with the jaws, the marked hole on the −y side of the line through the centre parallel to the jaws. A plate with a broken tap in one hole is still used for its other holes; the stub stays in that hole. Tap and wrench. Brush the swarf off the tap, re-wet its chamfer with aluminium tapping fluid, check the red band, and stand the wrench in its stand with the T-bar along x. Replace the tap after every 20 holes, or at once if it is broken or a tooth is chipped (about US$10). Swarf: Brush the aluminium chips out of the vise into a bin after each trial. Safety. Staff wear safety glasses, and gloves when handling a broken tap. The grippers touch only the wrench: Each pad wears a replaceable cover of 1 in polyimide tape, in case a pad meets the tap's flutes. The arm's forces cannot throw the parts. Time and cost: About 3 minutes per reset. The kit (vise, wrench, taps, gauge, parallels, square, feeler gauges) costs under US$300.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; cutting is a rule in task.py. The tap bites seated in the countersink, pushed 3 N, within 10 deg; drives then hold it on a 1 mm/turn helix. In its first turn its tilt just sticks (0.05 N m); the thread's axis is its mean over that turn. Turning in needs 0.8 N m plus 0.8 N m per turn cut since a 90 deg back-off. It snaps at 1.5 N m bending at the plate's face or 5 N m twist. Torques, bite push and snap limits are estimates. No chips, fluid or wear.
